chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who has a servant girl, and he says: 'She is for so-and-so to serve him as long as he lives, and when he dies, she is free.' The slave girl runs away (abiq) before the man dies, by five or six years. Then his heirs find her. Is it for them to use her after she has run away? He said: No. When the man dies, she has become free, so it does not contradict the first report, because the aspect of it is that the manumission (tadbir) had been attached to the time for which she was to serve him. Wherever she ran away, it prevented the man who was granted that authority over her, and that does not invalidate the manumission. And in the first report, the manumission was attached to the death of the master, so wherever her running away prevented her master from having authority over her, that invalidated that manumission. And that which confirms the first report.

key_terms.التّدبِير: Manumission of a slave upon the master's death
key_terms.الخَبَرَ الأَوّل: The first report (referring to a specific legal precedent)

ai.seo_question: Does a slave girl's running away before her master's death invalidate her manumission (tadbir)?
ai.summary: In this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the distinction is drawn between a 'mudabbir' whose manumission is contingent upon the master's death versus one contingent upon a specific duration of service; the Imam clarifies that her running away (ibaq) merely suspends the master's active control without voiding the underlying condition of death. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that the legal effect of manumission is tied to the occurrence of the specified event rather than continuous physical possession, ensuring the slave's freedom is preserved despite temporary absence. The hadith underscores the precision in distinguishing between conditions that are time-bound versus those bound to the master's lifespan, a key nuance in Usuli legal reasoning.
